title: The one who offers a leaf (9.11–9.25)
word: The one who offers a leaf
hook: a poor man brings the richest friend in the world a handful of flattened rice

segments.voice: Yesterday Krishna said, I will tell you the most secret, and the secret was wind resting in the sky. Your line was the secret. Today, what someone can bring to the one who holds everything. Day one hundred ninety.
screen: `"I WILL TELL YOU THE MOST SECRET" — THE SECRET.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells about Sudama, a poor Brahmin who had studied with Krishna as a boy. Years later Krishna is a king in a golden city, and Sudama's family has barely enough to eat. His wife begs him to go and visit his old friend. But what do you bring a king? Sudama borrows a few handfuls of flattened rice and ties them in a corner of his worn cloth. At the palace, Krishna runs to hug him, washes his feet, and then notices the little bundle he's trying to hide. What's that you've brought me?
screen: `A POOR MAN. A KING FOR A FRIEND.` → `A HANDFUL OF FLATTENED RICE.` → `WHAT'S THAT YOU'VE BROUGHT ME?`

segments.voice: In the story, Krishna takes the rice and eats it with delight, and he says a verse from the Gita. It's the verse that crowns today's reading: whoever offers me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, I accept that offering of love from the one whose heart is pure. That's Gita nine, twenty-six. Patram, pushpam, phalam, toyam. A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water. The four cheapest things in the world. Anyone can find them. The verses that lead up to it build the whole scene around that verse. Krishna has said fools look past him in human form. But great souls, verse fourteen says, are always singing about him, bowing, steady in their vows. He is the ritual and the offering, the fire and the ghee, verse sixteen. He is the father of the world, verse seventeen; the mother, the grandparent. He is the goal, the support, the lord, the witness, the home, the refuge, the friend. Then verse twenty-two, which many people know by heart: to those who worship me alone, always united with me, I bring what they lack and protect what they have. And so, when the Lord of everything gets to name what he wants, he names a leaf. Not because the gift is big, but because the love is real. The word the verse leans on is bhakti, devotion, love turned toward God. Sudama, the story says, walked home embarrassed he hadn't asked for anything, and found his hut had become a palace. That's today's word: the one who offers a leaf.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF RICE, EATEN WITH JOY.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `WHAT THEY LACK, I BRING.` · `NOT THE GIFT. THE LOVE.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO OFFERS A LEAF.`

segments.voice: If you can, get something small before you sit: a glass of water, a leaf from outside, a flower, a piece of fruit. If not, picture one. Hold it in your open hands. Breathe. Think of what you'd want to offer with it: thanks, a worry, a person you love. If you pray, you can offer it to God, as the verse says. If not, simply hold it with care, as if it were a gift. The bell holds the time.
The one who offers a leaf. Gita nine, twenty-six: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, offered with love, is accepted.
screen: `THE ONE WHO OFFERS A LEAF — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a leaf, a flower, water. Today, give one small thing with real love: a glass of water, a note, five minutes. Day one hundred ninety.

howItsDone: In daily puja many Hindus offer flowers, tulsi or bilva leaves, fruit and water at the home shrine; Gita 9.26 is often recited to explain that what matters is the love, not the size of the offering.

fork.setup: you're Sudama, at the palace of your childhood friend, now a king. all you have is a little flattened rice in your cloth. what do you do?
options: give it proudly, as a king's gift.
sell it to buy something better.
fork.reveal: he tries to hide it, and Krishna finds it and eats it with joy. the gift mattered because of the love, not the price.

original.note: Sanskrit: patram pushpam phalam toyam, a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water (Gita 9.26).

trapdoor: what you thought: worship needs gold and rituals.
what it means: a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, given with love, is enough; God brings what the devotee lacks.

what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata Purana (10th book) has Krishna recite Gita 9.26 to Sudama; 9.22's 'yoga-kshemam vahamy aham', I carry their welfare, is printed as a motto by the Life Insurance Corporation of India.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 9.22 (I bring what they lack)
